summary: This proposed standard defines a framework for extending SMTP so that a server can tell a client which optional features it supports. It is the basis for later SMTP extensions. It was replaced by RFC 1651.

eli5.summary: Email servers used to only know a few basic phrases. This paper lets a server say, I also understand these extra phrases, so new features can be added without breaking old ones.

questions: what does the ehlo command do
how can you add new features to smtp without breaking old programs
subtitle: A framework for adding new features to SMTP without breaking old implementations

tldr.problem: SMTP has been stable but unchangeable: adding new features risks breaking clients and servers that do not understand them. The protocol needed a way to evolve while remaining compatible with older implementations.
tldr.mechanism: A client can send the EHLO command instead of HELO to ask the server what optional features it supports. The server responds with a list of extension keywords. Both clients and servers can then choose to use extensions, and the IANA maintains a registry of standard extensions.
tldr.outcome: SMTP can now grow with new features (like 8-bit MIME support and authentication) without fragmenting into incompatible versions. RFC 1651 superseded this as an updated specification.

facts.label: Initial registry size
facts.value: 6 extensions (SEND, SOML, SAML, EXPN, HELP, TURN)

today: RFC 1425 is a Proposed Standard. It was superseded by RFC 1651, which made the same specification a Draft Standard. The EHLO command and framework for SMTP extensions have become fundamental to modern email systems.

sections.title: Introduction and Design Philosophy
sections.content:
The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP), defined in RFC 821, has been the standard for mail relay for over a decade. SMTP is strong because it is simple: clients and servers implement a core set of commands (HELO, MAIL, RCPT, DATA, RSET, VRFY, NOOP, QUIT), and this simplicity makes SMTP reliable and ubiquitous.

However, the Internet community identified the need for new features, such as delivery status notifications, message authentication, and support for 8-bit content. This RFC defines a framework for adding extensions to SMTP without requiring all existing clients and servers to change.

The key design principle is: protocols with few options tend toward ubiquity; protocols with many options tend toward obscurity. Each extension must be carefully evaluated. This RFC creates a framework so that extensions can be added in a consistent way, and a server can advertise which extensions it supports.
sections.eli5: Email is simple and works everywhere, but people wanted new features. The problem was: how do you add features without breaking all the old email programs? The answer is: ask first. A server says "I also understand these new things," and old programs just ignore it and keep working.

sections.title: The Extension Framework
sections.content:
The framework consists of three parts:

1. The EHLO command: A client supporting extensions sends EHLO (Extended HELO) instead of HELO at the start of an SMTP session. If the server supports extensions, it responds with code 250 and lists the extensions it provides. If the server does not support extensions, it responds with code 500 (command not recognized), and the client falls back to HELO and basic SMTP.

2. The IANA registry of extensions: Each standard extension is registered with IANA and has an EHLO keyword value (like SEND, SOML, SAML, EXPN, HELP, TURN). The initial registry includes optional SMTP commands from RFC 821.

3. Extended parameters for MAIL FROM and RCPT TO: Extensions can define additional parameters to the MAIL and RCPT commands, using a syntax like MAIL FROM: PARAM=value. All parameter keywords must be registered with IANA.
sections.eli5: The server says "I know these tricks." The client says "which tricks can you do?" The server lists them. The client says "okay, let us use trick X." Old clients just skip that conversation and use the old way.

sections.title: The EHLO Command and Response
sections.content:
A client sends EHLO <domain> instead of HELO <domain>. The domain is the client's host name (like ymir.claremont.edu).

A server that recognizes EHLO responds with code 250 and one or more lines listing the extensions. Each line contains an EHLO keyword (like EXPN, HELP, 8BITMIME) and optional parameters. Keywords may be upper, lower, or mixed case but are processed case-insensitively.

The response is a multi-line reply: the first line ends with a dash (250-), intermediate lines also end with a dash, and the last line ends with a space (250 ). Keywords starting with "X" are non-standard local extensions for bilateral agreement; all others must be registered with IANA.

A client MUST NOT cache the response. It must issue EHLO again at the start of each SMTP session, because the server capabilities may have changed (for example, due to a restart).
sections.eli5: The client asks "What can you do?" The server lists each ability on a line. Old tricks like SEND, SOML, HELP work, and new tricks get added as long as someone registers them.

sections.title: Error Handling
sections.content:
If a server does not recognize EHLO, it returns code 500 (bad command), and the client should send HELO and proceed with basic SMTP.

If the server recognizes EHLO but finds the argument unacceptable, it returns code 501 (syntax error in parameters). If the server recognizes EHLO but does not implement it, it returns code 502 (command not implemented). If the service is temporarily unavailable, it returns code 421.

For extended MAIL FROM or RCPT TO parameters, if the server does not recognize a parameter, it returns code 555. If the server recognizes the parameter but cannot accommodate it temporarily, it returns code 455. Specific errors for each parameter are defined in that parameter's RFC.
sections.eli5: If the server does not understand EHLO, the client just uses HELO instead. If the server understands it but rejects a parameter, it says so with a specific error code.

sections.title: The IANA Extension Registry
sections.content:
The initial IANA registry includes the optional SMTP commands from RFC 821: SEND, SOML (Send or Mail), SAML (Send and Mail), EXPN (Expand), HELP, and TURN. Each entry includes the EHLO keyword, any parameters, the associated SMTP verb, and the behavior it adds.

Standards-track RFCs can define new service extensions. Each must include: the textual name of the extension, the EHLO keyword, the syntax and values of parameters, any new SMTP verbs, any new parameters for MAIL FROM or RCPT TO, and how the extension affects client and server behavior.

The IANA maintains and publishes this registry. Conforming servers must not offer non-"X" prefixed keywords that are not in the registry. Extensions are expected to be documented in standards-track RFCs, ensuring careful review and community consensus before they are added to the Internet standard.
sections.eli5: IANA (the organization that assigns Internet numbers) keeps a list of official tricks. Anyone can propose a new trick, but it has to be reviewed and approved before it is official.
